title: Angle Relationships

findings.finding: Generalise the distinction between alternative names and distinct geometrical objects.
findings.breakdown: The existing question contrasts coincident rays with different segments; counting all objects extends that comparison naturally.
findings.checked: For collinear P, Q, R in that order, the six ordered names determine one line, four rays and three segments. The definitions and p4-q3 supply the required methods.
findings.assumptions: P, Q and R are distinct, with Q between P and R.

repair.proposal: After p4-q3-b, optionally ask: 'Using two different letters from P, Q and R, name every distinct line, ray and segment. Group names for the same object and explain.' Expected: one line with six names; four rays, PQ=PR, RP=RQ, QP and QR; three segments, PQ=QP, PR=RP and QR=RQ.

findings.doneWhen: The task distinguishes names from objects and includes the correct grouping.

findings.finding: Question 3 requires relating a whole angle to its adjacent component sectors, but preceding instruction does not supply that relationship.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise which label measures the whole angle and decide whether to add component measures or subtract a known component. The adjacency definition supplies positional conditions, without explaining this numerical relationship.
findings.checked: p5 and p6 identify whole-angle boundaries across internal arms but do not calculate measures. p10-q9-c–e already require sector addition, but provide no instructional cue or demonstration. p16 adds measures of separate angles for classification; p19 teaches adjacency only. General whole-angle addition and subtraction are not modelled before p21-q3.
findings.assumptions: This finding assumes angle decomposition has not been taught separately; retained context question q2 checks that assumption. Basic arithmetic is prior knowledge; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p21-q3, state: 'The measure of a whole angle is the sum of its adjacent parts.' Show sectors 32° and 47° inside a whole angle t°: t=32+47=79°. Then show a whole angle of 79°, one part 47° and the other x°: x+47=79, so x=79−47=32°. Explicitly identify the whole and its parts.

findings.doneWhen: Students see both finding a whole angle and finding a missing component modelled before Question 3, unless separate prior teaching establishes this method.

findings.finding: Distinguish adjacency from complementarity and supplementarity.
findings.breakdown: The task connects consecutive topics while separating a positional relationship from relationships between measures.
findings.checked: All three requested configurations exist: adjacent sectors 30° and 60°, 70° and 110°, and 40° and 60°. Definitions in p16 and p19 suffice.
findings.assumptions: Drawn sectors share a vertex and an arm without overlapping.

repair.proposal: After p20-q2, optionally ask: 'Draw and label (a) adjacent complementary angles, (b) adjacent supplementary angles, and (c) adjacent angles that are neither. Must adjacent angles be complementary or supplementary? Explain.' Expected examples: 30° and 60°; 70° and 110°; 40° and 60°. No: adjacency describes position, whereas complementarity and supplementarity describe totals.

findings.doneWhen: Students provide valid configurations and explain why adjacency alone does not determine the sum.

findings.finding: Justify vertically opposite equality using straight-angle relationships.
findings.breakdown: Students explain an established rule using previously taught relationships rather than measurement.
findings.checked: For two distinct intersecting lines, an angle c adjacent to both opposite angles gives a+c=180 and b+c=180, hence a=b. p22 supplies the straight-angle relationship and p32 supplies opposite-angle identification.
findings.assumptions: The two lines are distinct and intersect.

repair.proposal: After p34-q5, optionally ask: 'Two straight lines intersect. Label one angle a°, its vertically opposite angle b°, and an angle adjacent to both c°. Explain why a=b without measuring.' Expected: a+c=180 and b+c=180, so a=180−c=b.

findings.doneWhen: The explanation derives opposite-angle equality from the two straight-angle equations.

findings.finding: Parts b and i repeat the same whole parallelism task without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both ask for a parallelism decision and justification from the same 124° and 46° co-interior givens in the same configuration.
findings.checked: Compared the shared stem, complete parts, supplied diagram descriptions, angle positions and givens. Both have two descending steep lines crossed by a descending transversal, six continuation arrows, and the same marked interior sectors. No retrieval or comparison instruction explains the repetition.
findings.assumptions: The supplied diagram specifications represent the repeated configuration accurately.
findings.doneWhen: Question 6 contains one copy of the 124° and 46° co-interior parallelism task.

findings.finding: Generalise the angle between the bisectors of adjacent angles.
findings.breakdown: The existing equal-angle pairs provide the structure needed to explain when the two bisecting rays are perpendicular.
findings.checked: For positive adjacent angles a and b with total θ<360°, the smaller angle between their internal bisectors is a/2+b/2=θ/2. It equals 90° exactly when θ=180°. The existing question supplies equal halves, and earlier teaching supplies angle addition.
findings.assumptions: Both angles are positive, have disjoint interiors and together span less than a complete turn.

repair.proposal: After p77-q22, optionally ask: 'Two positive adjacent angles total θ°, where 0<θ<360. Draw a ray dividing each angle into two equal parts. Find the smaller angle between these rays, explain your answer, and state when they are perpendicular.' Expected: θ/2, because the intervening halves sum to a/2+b/2; perpendicular exactly when θ=180°.

findings.doneWhen: The task states its angle conditions and derives both θ/2 and the perpendicularity condition.

contextQuestions.question: Before labelling angles, have students learnt to recognise the reflex sector between two arms and distinguish it from the smaller sector? The supplied preceding teaching models smaller marked angles but does not teach the reflex instruction used here.

Have students already been taught that a whole angle's measure is the sum of its adjacent component measures, including finding a missing component by subtraction? Separate prior teaching would change the retained unsupported-transition finding.
